THOUGHT: The patient developed repetitive, stereotyped tapping of the right hand beginning on day 5 after an acute left thalamic infarct. Key phenomenology: repetitive, highly patterned movements; duration 30 seconds–5 minutes; the patient can voluntarily suppress them; no premonitory urge or internal tension before movements; no impairment of awareness, incontinence, or EEG abnormalities; the movements gradually waned and nearly resolved by 1 month. These features best fit a focal post‑stroke motor stereotypy arising from a thalamic lesion (thalamic and basal ganglia circuitry commonly produce contralateral stereotypies). Focal motor seizures (automatisms) are an important differential but usually have more abrupt onset, shorter stereotyped events, often impaired awareness and/or EEG correlate (though EEG can be normal); the ability to suppress and preserved awareness argue against typical epileptic automatisms. Tics are suppressible but are typically accompanied by a premonitory urge and are less likely to have new onset in mid‑adult life localized to a single hand after a focal stroke. Chorea/hemiballismus or focal dystonia from basal ganglia/thalamic lesions can follow stroke but their phenomenology (irregular non‑stereotyped jerks for chorea/ballism, sustained abnormal postures for dystonia) differs from the described rhythmic tapping. Functional (psychogenic) movements remain a possibility but are less likely because of close temporal relation to an acute structural lesion and the stereotyped, stimulus‑independent pattern that resolved as the acute stroke evolved.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Post‑stroke focal motor stereotypy (right‑hand stereotypy) due to acute left thalamic infarct
2. Focal epileptic automatisms / focal motor seizures (frontal/temporal origin) — less likely but important alternative
3. Acquired simple motor tic (focal tic disorder) — atypical because of age of onset and lack of premonitory urge
4. Post‑stroke hyperkinetic movement such as hemichorea/hemiballismus or focal dystonia secondary to basal ganglia/thalamic involvement
5. Functional (psychogenic) movement disorder

Case Information:
A man in his 40s presented with sudden-onset slurring of speech and imbalance on walking. He had difficulty swallowing and required a nasogastric tube for feeding. Six months previously, he had left-sided hemiparesis, which had improved significantly. On day 5 of admission, purposeless tapping movements were observed in the patient's right hand. The movements were repetitive, of the same type, and lasted for 30 seconds to 5 minutes. The patient was able to suppress these movements at will. These movements were not preceded by an urge to perform them, and on stopping, there was no development of internal tension. The movements were not associated with any change in sensorium or incontinence. The movements slowly decreased in severity but maintained the same pattern. He was discharged on day 28 when the movements were very mild. At the 1-month follow-up, the movements had almost disappeared.

Physical Examination:
The patient demonstrated repetitive tapping movements in the right hand that could be voluntarily suppressed.

Diagnostic Tests:
- Imaging Studies:    Image Title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging of the Brain    Image Description: T1, T2, diffusion-weighted, and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) axial images showing:    - Acute infarct in left thalamic region (isointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, hyperintense on diffusion, hypointense on ADC)    - Old infarct in right gangliocapsular region        - Other Tests:    Electroencephalogram (day 7): No abnormalities        - Video Documentation:    Title: Right Hand Stereotypy    Description: Stereotypic movements of the right hand in the form of repeated tapping; patient able to stop the tapping when asked to do so
